claims.text: Failed child, CPython 3.13 docs: TaskGroup cancels the remaining tasks the first time a child fails with an exception other than CancelledError, and no further tasks can be added. gather (return_exceptions=False, default) immediately propagates the first raised exception to the awaiting task, but the other awaitables are NOT cancelled and keep running. The gather docs note says TaskGroup gives stronger safety guarantees because it cancels remaining tasks on failure and gather does not. With gather(return_exceptions=True), exceptions are returned as ordinary results in the list.

TaskGroup: the async with statement waits for all tasks in the group to finish (all tasks are awaited when the context manager exits). New tasks may still be added while waiting, for example by a child using tg.create_task, until the last task has finished and the block exits. After a failure it cancels the remaining tasks and then waits for them to finish before raising. gather: on full success it returns an aggregate list in input order, so it covers all awaitables. In the default mode it stops waiting at the first exception, which is propagated immediately while the siblings keep running unawaited by that call. With return_exceptions=True, exceptions count as results and the list is aggregated. The supplied extract does not explicitly say that gather waits for every awaitable in the return_exceptions=True case; that is only implied by the aggregate result.

TaskGroup groups failures: once all tasks have finished, any exceptions other than CancelledError are combined into an ExceptionGroup or BaseExceptionGroup (as appropriate) and raised. Exceptions to this: (a) if a task fails with KeyboardInterrupt or SystemExit, the group still cancels and waits for the remaining tasks, but then re-raises the initial KeyboardInterrupt or SystemExit instead of a group. (b) CancelledError is not included in the group; this includes a CancelledError passed to __aexit__ from the body. (c) If the body of the async with exits with an exception, it is treated like a child failure: siblings are cancelled and awaited, and the body exception is included in the group, except CancelledError, with the same KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit special case. (d) If the group is cancelled externally and must also raise an ExceptionGroup, it calls the parent task's cancel() so the cancellation is not lost. gather, by contrast, propagates the first raised exception itself and does not group them.

In gather, if an individual Task or Future in aws is cancelled, it is treated as if it raised CancelledError, and the gather() call itself is NOT cancelled. This is intended to prevent cancelling one submitted Task/Future from causing the other tasks to be cancelled. Contrast: if gather() itself is cancelled, all submitted awaitables that have not completed are also cancelled (propagated regardless of return_exceptions since 3.7). Caveat: with return_exceptions=False, cancelling gather after it is already marked done, for example after it propagated an exception, does not cancel any submitted awaitables. The extract does not spell out how the per-child CancelledError is surfaced to the caller (raised versus placed in the result list) beyond the 'treated as if it raised CancelledError' wording.

Cancellation is delivered by raising asyncio.CancelledError in the task at the next opportunity. The docs say a caught CancelledError should generally be propagated after clean-up, and that CancelledError subclasses BaseException so ordinary 'except Exception' code does not catch it. The structured-concurrency components TaskGroup and asyncio.timeout() are implemented using cancellation internally and might misbehave if a coroutine swallows CancelledError. If suppression is truly desired, uncancel() must also be called to fully remove the cancellation state; user code should not generally call uncancel(). TaskGroup also relies on preserved cancellation counts (Task.cancelling()), and in 3.13 it improved handling of simultaneous internal and external cancellation. The docs do not list concrete failure modes such as hangs or timeouts that never fire; that elaboration is not sourced.

Recommendation: for all-or-cancel sibling work, use asyncio.TaskGroup. It cancels siblings on the first non-cancellation failure, waits for them, and raises an ExceptionGroup. gather(return_exceptions=False) leaves siblings running after the first exception. Version caveat: TaskGroup was added in Python 3.11, and the ExceptionGroup it raises is also not available before 3.11 per the docs' usage here (only TaskGroup's versionadded 3.11 is sourced). On Python 3.10 or older, TaskGroup is unavailable and gather would need manual cancellation of siblings. On 3.13, TaskGroup.create_task closes the coroutine if the group is inactive and cancellation-count handling is improved; callers on 3.11-3.12 may not have those 3.13 changes. Callers must handle ExceptionGroup, for example with except*.

recommendation: Use asyncio.TaskGroup on Python 3.11 or later for all-or-cancel sibling work. Prefer 3.13 for its improved cancellation handling. Handle the resulting ExceptionGroup, for example with except*. Never swallow CancelledError inside children. If it must be suppressed, call uncancel() deliberately. Use gather only when siblings may keep running after a failure, or with return_exceptions=True when all results are wanted. On versions before 3.11, TaskGroup is unavailable, so cancel siblings manually.
